strengths: The paper presents a unified and principled framework that elegantly connects classical search principles (BFS, DFS) with modern diffusion model inference-time compute scaling.
A key theoretical contribution is Proposition 1 and Theorem 1, which formally connects training-free recurrence-based guidance with annealed Langevin MCMC, providing a rigorous convergence bound.
The proposed DFS-style non-linear search is highly innovative, showing the capability to adaptively allocate computational resources based on instance difficulty without prior knowledge.

Comprehensive empirical evaluations across diverse domains—including planning (PointMaze), offline reinforcement learning (D4RL), and text-to-image synthesis (CompBench)—demonstrate significant improvements over existing baselines.

The paper addresses a very practical issue of reward hacking/over-optimization using a novel double-verifier strategy (analogous to double Q-learning), leading to robust out-of-distribution performance.
weaknesses: The method introduces multiple hyperparameters (such as thresholds, step sizes, backtracking depth, and tempering schedules), which may limit its ease of use in new domains.

While the paper shows Pareto curves in terms of Number of Function Evaluations (NFEs), there is little discussion of actual wall-clock time overhead, which can be significant due to sequential backtracking and MCMC operations.
A few minor typographical errors are present in the figures (e.g., 'Parero Curves' in Figure 4, and 'successfual' in Figure 5).

strengths: Provides a comprehensive, unified framework that harmonizes global search (BFS, DFS) and local search (annealed Langevin MCMC) for diffusion model inference-time scaling.

Establishes a solid theoretical bridge (Proposition 1 and Theorem 1) proving that training-free recurrence guidance converges to Langevin MCMC in the continuous limit, which mathematically justifies why recurrence prevents out-of-distribution (OOD) generation.
Introduces an adaptive Depth-First Search (DFS) algorithm with backtracking that dynamically allocates compute based on instance difficulty, improving efficiency by up to 2x over BFS baselines.

Extensive empirical validation across diverse domains including text-to-image generation, long-horizon maze planning, and offline reinforcement learning, consistently outperforming established baselines.
Proposes a simple yet highly effective double-verifier strategy to mitigate reward hacking and over-optimization during gradient-guided local search.
weaknesses: The search framework introduces several critical hyperparameters (e.g., backtracking depth $\Delta_T$, budget $B$, threshold schedules $\delta_t$, and verifier weight $\lambda$). Tuning these across different tasks can be highly complex and sensitive, which may limit the generalizability and ease of use in new domains.

The computational overhead of test-time scaling is inherently high, requiring multiple denoising passes, gradient computations, and backtracks. While the paper reports compute in NFEs, a detailed discussion or table of wall-clock time latency would be beneficial to assess the viability for real-time applications like robotics.

The method heavily relies on the availability of robust verifier functions. While the double-verifier strategy helps, if the base verifiers are noisy, biased, or poorly calibrated, the search process could still lead to suboptimal generations or suffer from more advanced forms of reward hacking.

The comparison with concurrent search-based scaling methods (such as ABCD or EvoSearch) is limited to qualitative discussions in the appendix; quantitative comparisons with these concurrent approaches would make the empirical evaluation even more robust.

strengths: Grounds diffusion model inference-time scaling in classical search theory, unifying prior work (such as SMC and training-free guidance) under a clean BFS/DFS and local/global search taxonomy.

Proposes Proposition 1 and Theorem 1, establishing a rigorous theoretical connection between training-free guidance with recurrence and annealed Langevin MCMC, which explains why recurrence mitigates out-of-distribution artifacts.
Introduces an adaptive DFS algorithm with backtracking that dynamically allocates compute based on instance difficulty, showcasing superior efficiency over fixed schedules.

Demonstrates strong empirical results across three distinct and challenging domains: text-to-image generation (CompBench, ImageNet), long-horizon planning (PointMaze), and offline reinforcement learning (D4RL).
Addresses the practical issue of verifier over-optimization (reward hacking) by proposing a novel, highly effective double-verifier strategy inspired by double Q-learning.
weaknesses: The search-based and iterative gradient guidance methods introduce significant computational overhead (high Number of Function Evaluations - NFEs), which might limit their deployment in real-time or latency-sensitive applications.

The proposed framework introduces several new hyperparameters (backtracking depth, score thresholds, local search step size, etc.) which can be sensitive and require task-specific tuning, as shown in the appendix.

strengths: Proposes a clean, elegant, and unified framework that categorizes inference-time scaling of diffusion models into local search (via Langevin MCMC) and global search (via tree search like BFS/DFS).

Provides a valuable theoretical contribution (Proposition 1) that mathematically unifies training-free guidance with recurrence and annealed Langevin MCMC in the continuous limit, explaining why recurrence prevents out-of-distribution drift.

Evaluates the method across a wide and diverse range of applications including long-horizon maze planning, offline RL (D4RL), compositional text-to-image generation (CompBench), and conditional ImageNet generation.
Introduces an intuitive DFS-based global search strategy that leverages 'renoising' (backtracking) and adaptively scales compute depending on prompt difficulty.
Addresses the critical problem of verifier hacking (adversarial generation) by proposing a simple yet effective double-verifier scheme.
weaknesses: Some individual search components (such as BFS-style particle filtering/resampling) have been similarly explored in concurrent or recent literature (e.g., Sequential Monte Carlo steering), which slightly reduces the standalone novelty of the global BFS search block.

The proposed search algorithms introduce several hyperparameters (such as temperature $\tau_t$, evaluation schedules $S$, backtracking depth $\Delta_T$, and threshold schedules $\delta_t$) that require careful tuning and can be task-dependent.

The computational overhead (wall-clock time) introduced by frequently evaluating the verifier networks (e.g., BLIP-VQA, UniDet) at intermediate timesteps is not comprehensively analyzed relative to the gain in performance.

The conditional ImageNet evaluation is limited to only two class labels (222 and 444), which is quite small and makes it hard to fully generalize the FID and accuracy improvements across the entire dataset.

strengths: The paper successfully unifies local search (via gradient-based Langevin MCMC) and global search (via BFS/DFS) for diffusion models. The theoretical connection (Proposition 1) between training-free recurrence guidance and Langevin MCMC is clean and provides strong motivation.

The method is evaluated across highly diverse domains: long-horizon planning (PointMaze), offline RL (D4RL), and text-to-image generation (CompBench, ImageNet). This broad evaluation demonstrates the general applicability of the search framework.
The DFS-based backtracking strategy is a clever way to adaptively scale inference-time compute, automatically allocating more budget to harder prompts/scenarios without manual tuning.
The introduction of the double-verifier technique to mitigate 'verifier hacking' is a very practical and effective contribution to the problem of classifier-guided generation.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with high-quality, intuitive figures (Figures 1 and 2) and clear pseudo-code (Algorithms 1-4) that make the proposed methods easy to understand.
weaknesses: The proposed algorithms introduce several hyperparameters (e.g., backtracking depth, threshold schedules, temperature, number of particles, evaluation steps). The paper lacks a detailed sensitivity analysis to show how robust the performance is to variations in these parameters.

The theoretical equivalence in Proposition 1 is proven in the continuous-time limit (as the number of steps T goes to infinity). In practice, diffusion models are run with a small, discrete number of steps, and the impact of the discretization error on this theoretical equivalence is not discussed.

In the offline RL experiments on D4RL, the authors do not apply BFS or DFS and instead use simple Best-of-N due to the small number of particles. This leaves the benefit of structured global tree search on decision-making tasks somewhat under-explored compared to the image and planning tasks.

strengths: Theoretically grounded unification: The paper provides a nice theoretical unification of training-free guidance with recurrence and annealed Langevin MCMC (Proposition 1), showing that recurrence acts as a Langevin drift pulling samples back to the data manifold.

Well-designed search algorithms: The adaptation of classical BFS and DFS search algorithms to the continuous denoising space of diffusion models is logical and well-formulated. In particular, the DFS-based backtracking mechanism successfully enables adaptive, difficulty-aware compute allocation.

Diverse and challenging benchmarks: The method is validated across three distinct and challenging domains—long-horizon maze planning, offline reinforcement learning, and text-to-image generation—consistently showing improvements in performance and compute efficiency.

Clever mitigation of verifier hacking: The introduction of the double-verifier technique (inspired by double Q-learning) is a practical and effective solution to address the adversarial vulnerability of classifier-based guidance.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty over Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) steering: BFS-style resampling has been previously explored in several works under the guise of Sequential Monte Carlo or Feynman-Kac steering. The paper could do a better job of highlighting the precise differences and improvements of BFS-Resampling/Pruning over these existing methods.

Evaluation of verifier computation cost: The paper measures compute efficiency primarily using Number of Function Evaluations (NFEs) of the diffusion model. However, evaluating complex verifiers (e.g., BLIP-VQA or UniDet) at multiple intermediate steps can introduce significant computational and latency overheads. A more holistic analysis of the wall-clock time or computational cost including the verifier calls would strengthen the paper.

Sensitivity to hyperparameters: The proposed search strategies introduce many hyperparameters (e.g., evaluation steps $S$, temperature $\tau_t$, backtracking depth $\Delta_T$, threshold schedule $\delta_t$). Tuning these across different tasks and verifiers can be challenging, which may limit the ease of deployment in new domains.
